title: How To Improve Classroom Management By Talking Less https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2011/04/16/improve-classroom-management-by-talking-less/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that teachers who narrate and manage every moment of the school day with constant talk actually make classroom management harder, not easier. Excessive talking causes students to tune out, weakens the meaning of a teacher's words, signals distrust, and creates tension. He offers six concrete tactics for talking less: leaning on a classroom management plan instead of verbal reminders, teaching procedures thoroughly, refusing to repeat directions, speaking only when necessary, practicing brevity, and simply observing more instead of narrating. He also connects reduced talking to stronger relationships, since quieter teachers have more bandwidth to actually get to know their students. The piece closes with a direct challenge to cut talking by a third to gain more authority and calm.
points: Constant teacher talk undermines management by causing students to tune out and weakening the impact of words.
A well-taught classroom management plan and thoroughly modeled procedures let the system do the talking instead of the teacher.
Repeating directions trains students to ignore the first (and second, and third) request.
Brevity and observation, rather than narration, build a more mature, independent classroom.
Reducing talk time frees up capacity to build authentic rapport with students.
quotes: Many teachers make the mistake of trying to talk their students through each moment of the school day.
But it doesn’t work. Too much talking has the opposite effect. It makes classroom management more difficult.
When you let your classroom management plan do your talking for you, you can eliminate lecturing, pleading, yelling, scolding, arguing, and the like from your school day.
Many teachers repeat everything they say–sometimes three and four times. When you repeat yourself, you weaken your words and encourage students to ignore you.
The more efficient and direct you can be with your words, the more effective your teaching will be.
By limiting the amount of talking you do, you’ll have more time to get to know your students.
My challenge is to use the suggestions above to try cutting your talking by a third. If you do, you’ll find yourself speaking with more power and impact.
